title: Astraea Redux
alternative_titles: Astraea Redux: A Poem on the Happy Restoration & Return of His Sacred Majesty Charles the Second
description: Dryden's first public poem, celebrating the Restoration of Charles II in May 1660 and announcing the young poet's allegiance to the returning monarchy; it recasts the civil wars as a national illness now cured by the king's return.
plot_or_argument: The poem traces the disorder of the Interregnum, praises General Monck's role, and celebrates Charles II as the providential healer of the nation, drawing on biblical and classical typology.
narrative_structure: A panegyric in three movements: the diagnosis of national disorder, the mechanism of restoration, and the prophetic blessing on the new reign.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in closed iambic pentameter, with occasional alexandrines; one of the earliest displays of Dryden's mature couplet.
historical_context: Written within weeks of Charles II's landing at Dover on 25 May 1660 and published in the same year.
literary_significance: Established Dryden's public reputation and set the tone for the political panegyric of the Restoration; a benchmark for his later development.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Dryden on the title page of the 1660 quarto; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1660. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., Oxford University Press, 1958); also in The Works of John Dryden (University of California Press, 1956- ).

title: Annus Mirabilis
alternative_titles: Annus Mirabilis: The Year of Wonders 1666
description: Dryden's long historical poem on the two disasters of 1666 — the Second Anglo-Dutch War and the Great Fire of London — written from Charlton in Wiltshire, offering the nation an optimistic, providential reading of catastrophe.
plot_or_argument: The poem narrates the naval victories over the Dutch, then the Fire, and concludes with a prophecy of London's rebirth as a greater commercial empire under Charles II.
narrative_structure: A two-part public narrative (war, fire) framed by dedication and prophetic conclusion, with episodic set-pieces for individual battles.
meter_and_prosody: Quatrains (alternately rhymed iambic pentameter, ABAB), deliberately chosen over couplets to imitate the stateliness of history writing.
historical_context: Composed while Dryden was absent from plague-stricken London; dedicated to the City of London in the year of the Great Fire, and closely engaged with the Royal Society's new empiricism.
literary_significance: The major English public poem of the 1660s; it demonstrates Dryden's ability to turn current events into national myth and anticipates the scientific imagery of his later verse.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1667. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Absalom and Achitophel
description: Dryden's masterpiece of political satire, mapping the Exclusion Crisis onto the biblical story of Absalom's rebellion against David: Monmouth as Absalom, Shaftesbury as Achitophel, Charles II as David, and the Duke of York as the lawful successor.
plot_or_argument: Achitophel seduces the ambitious Absalom into rebellion against his indulgent father David; the poem culminates in David's assertion of divine-right authority and the rout of the Whig opposition.
narrative_structure: A two-part argumentative narrative: the diagnosis of national faction, then a series of extended character portraits, closing with the king's speech and the restoration of order.
principal_characters: David (Charles II); Absalom (James, Duke of Monmouth); Achitophel (Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury); Zimri (George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham); Corah (Titus Oates); Israel (the English people)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets; the most supple and rhetorically varied use of the closed couplet in seventeenth-century English.
historical_context: Published in November 1681 at the height of the Exclusion Crisis, apparently at the king's suggestion, and immediately answered by Settle and Shadwell.
literary_significance: Universally regarded as the greatest political poem in English; it created the model of the allegorical verse satire that Pope would inherit, and its character portraits remain a landmark of satirical psychology.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed, though Dryden claimed the plan was the king's.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1681, with Dryden's postscript of the same year. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958); The Works of John Dryden, vols. I-II (California, 1956- ).

title: Absalom and Achitophel, Part II
description: The continuation of Dryden's satire, largely written by Nahum Tate with Dryden supplying the portraits of Achitophel and the closing sections; it attacks Settle and Shadwell as Doeg and Og.
plot_or_argument: The sequel extends the biblical allegory into the trials of the Whig leaders and the vindication of David's government, adding a second book that completes Tate's unfinished first part.
narrative_structure: Two parts: Tate's first book of about 550 lines and Dryden's second book of about 450 lines.
principal_characters: Doeg (Thomas Shadwell); Og (Elkanah Settle); Achitophel (Earl of Shaftesbury); Corah (Titus Oates)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets.
historical_context: Published in November 1682, in the wake of Shaftesbury's flight and the Tory reaction; it answers Shadwell's The Medal of John Bayes.
literary_significance: Important chiefly for Dryden's contribution, which contains the famous second portrait of Achitophel and the Doeg-Og passage; the whole is far less read than Part I.
attribution_notes: The 1682 title page names Tate and Dryden; modern scholarship assigns the first book to Tate and the second to Dryden, with Dryden also revising Tate's text.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1682. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Mac Flecknoe
alternative_titles: Mac Flecknoe: A Satire upon the True-blew-Protestant Poet, T. S.
description: Dryden's short mock-heroic satire on Thomas Shadwell, imagining the dull poet Richard Flecknoe abdicating his empire of nonsense and choosing Shadwell as his heir.
plot_or_argument: Flecknoe, monarch of the realm of dullness, delivers a coronation speech naming Shadwell as his successor; Shadwell is crowned amid burlesque pomp and vanishes through a trapdoor.
narrative_structure: A single continuous mock-coronation scene in elevated epic diction, ending with the sudden comic collapse of the hero.
principal_characters: Richard Flecknoe; Thomas Shadwell (Sh—-); Henry VIII's ghost; Arion
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets used to comic effect by sustaining an epic register throughout.
historical_context: Written between about 1678 and 1682, circulated in manuscript, and printed without Dryden's name in 1682; it arises from the quarrel over dramatic criticism that began with The Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
literary_significance: The first sustained mock-heroic in English and the direct model for Pope's The Dunciad; it established the 'empire of dullness' conceit that dominated Augustan satire.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1682 and ascribed to Dryden by contemporaries; attribution undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1682; attributed to Dryden in Tonson's 1716 miscellany. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: The Medal
alternative_titles: The Medal: A Satire against Sedition
description: Dryden's angry direct satire, provoked by the Whig medal struck to honour Shaftesbury after his acquittal on the charge of high treason; it abandons allegory for open invective.
plot_or_argument: The poem denounces Shaftesbury and the City of London as seditious, attacks the doctrine of popular sovereignty, and closes with a prophetic address to the king urging firm government.
narrative_structure: A three-part invective: the medal and its meaning, the character of the Whig leaders, and the concluding political doctrine.
principal_characters: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury; the 'true-blue Protestant' crowd
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets.
historical_context: Published in March 1682, shortly after Shaftesbury's acquittal by the Old Bailey jury in November 1681; it drew Shadwell's reply The Medal of John Bayes.
literary_significance: The most forthright of Dryden's political satires and an important document of Tory argument in the Exclusion Crisis.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1682. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Religio Laici
alternative_titles: Religio Laici: or, A Layman's Faith
description: Dryden's philosophical poem defending the Anglican via media against both Catholic tradition and Protestant private judgement, written while he was still a conforming member of the Church of England.
plot_or_argument: The poem argues that Scripture is the sole rule of faith but is obscure in places, that private interpretation leads to chaos, and that the established church's tradition supplies the necessary authority.
narrative_structure: A continuous argumentative poem with a prose preface defending its 'fugitive' method and rough verse.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, deliberately roughened, with frequent alexandrines and triplets.
historical_context: Published in November 1682, after Dryden's translation of Simon's Criticial History; it responds to the Deist and Socinian challenge to revelation.
literary_significance: A key text in the history of English apologetics and the immediate predecessor of Pope's Essay on Man; it also marks the religious position Dryden abandoned when he converted to Catholicism in 1685-6.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1682. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: The Hind and the Panther
alternative_titles: The Hind and the Panther: A Poem in Three Parts
description: Dryden's great beast-fable of religious controversy, written after his conversion to Roman Catholicism: the milk-white Hind (the Roman Church) is pursued and slandered by the Panther (the Church of England) and the other beasts of the English sects.
plot_or_argument: The Hind, immortal and unafathed, seeks her lost children; she debates authority and interpretation with the Panther, recounts her own conversion, and the poem ends with the fable of the Swallows and the Martins.
narrative_structure: Three parts: the characters of the beasts, the theological debate at the Hind's house, and the concluding fable; framed by an extended address to the poem itself.
principal_characters: the Hind (the Roman Catholic Church); the Panther (the Church of England); the Bear (Independents); the Hare (Quakers); the Wolf (Presbyterians); the Ape (Freethinkers); the Swallow (Titus Oates)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of sustained eloquence, with the most complex syntax of Dryden's verse.
historical_context: Published in April 1687 under the Declaration of Indulgence, when James II's policy of toleration for Catholics briefly encouraged open Catholic argument; it was parodied within weeks by Montagu and Prior in The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd.
literary_significance: The longest and most serious of Dryden's poems and the fullest statement of his Catholic apologetic; a masterpiece of sustained argumentative verse that influenced Pope's Essay on Man.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1687. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: To the Memory of Mr. Oldham
description: Dryden's elegy for the young satirist John Oldham, who died of smallpox in December 1683; a short masterpiece of restrained praise that compares Oldham's early death to that of Marcellus and Nisus.
plot_or_argument: The poem laments the loss of a kindred wit, concedes the difference in style between the two poets, and consoles with the thought that Oldham's early death spared him the decay of age and dulness.
narrative_structure: A single continuous elegiac meditation of twenty-seven lines.
principal_characters: John Oldham; the speaker; Marcellus (alluded to)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets with frequent enjambment and a deliberately unpolished, masculine roughness suited to the subject.
historical_context: Written in the winter of 1683-4 and prefixed to the 1684 edition of Oldham's Works.
literary_significance: Often judged the finest short elegy in English between Lycidas and In Memoriam, and a canonical instance of Dryden's capacity for personal warmth.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1684. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Threnodia Augustalis
description: Dryden's funeral ode on the death of Charles II in February 1685, a public lament that mourns the king and welcomes the accession of James II.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with an ominous vision of a bleeding comet, narrates the king's last illness and death, laments the nation's loss, and turns to consolation in the new reign.
narrative_structure: A Pindaric sequence of irregular stanzas moving from omen through narrative to consolation.
principal_characters: Charles II; James II; the mourning nation
meter_and_prosody: Irregular Pindaric stanzas with varying line lengths and rhyme schemes.
historical_context: Written within weeks of Charles II's death on 6 February 1685 and printed in the same year.
literary_significance: A significant example of the Restoration public ode and of Dryden's adaptation of Cowley's Pindaric form to serious occasion.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1685. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: A Song for St. Cecilia's Day, 1687
description: Dryden's first Cecilia ode, a Neoplatonic hymn tracing the creation of the world through the music of the spheres to the final dissolution of all things by the last trumpet.
plot_or_argument: From discordant atoms, tuned by the voice of God, a harmonious universe arises; the stanzas then praise successive instruments and their passions, ending with the dread trumpet of the Last Judgement.
narrative_structure: Six stanzas plus a grand chorus, each stanza devoted to a different instrument or affect of music.
meter_and_prosody: A regular stanzaic form in mixed line lengths, with the famous four-beat 'The trumpet's loud clangour' passage.
historical_context: Written for the London celebrations of St Cecilia's Day on 22 November 1687 and set to music by Giovanni Battista Draghi.
literary_significance: One of the great English odes on music and the predecessor of Alexander's Feast; it became a staple of the choral repertoire through Handel and Purcell settings.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1687. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Alexander's Feast; or, The Power of Music
description: Dryden's second Cecilia ode, a dramatic narrative of the Greek musician Timotheus singing at Alexander the Great's victory feast and rousing him through pity, love, and finally revenge.
plot_or_argument: Timotheus's song moves Alexander from triumph to tears to drunken fury, so that he burns Persepolis; the poem concludes that a nobler master of harmony — St Cecilia — raised the sacred organ and the divine affections.
narrative_structure: A continuous dramatic narrative in irregular stanzas, ending with an abrupt change of key in the final chorus.
principal_characters: Alexander the Great; Timotheus; Thaïs; St Cecilia
meter_and_prosody: Irregular Pindaric stanzas; Dryden claimed to have written it in a single night and considered it his best work.
historical_context: Written for the Music Society's St Cecilia's Day celebration of 1697 and set by Jeremiah Clarke.
literary_significance: The culminating English ode of the seventeenth century; Handel's 1736 setting made it internationally famous and it remained a touchstone for poetic theories of versification through the eighteenth century.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1697. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Eleonora: A Panegyrical Dedication
description: Dryden's commissioned character-poem on an unnamed lady, written for the Earl of Abingdon in memory of his wife, whom the poem calls only Eleonora.
plot_or_argument: The poem sets out to describe Eleonora's virtues in an ordered portrait of her soul, mind, and conduct, and concedes the impossibility of doing her justice in verse.
narrative_structure: A panegyrical character study in a continuous argument, deliberately refusing narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets.
historical_context: Composed in 1691-2 for a fee of £100 from the Earl of Abingdon; Dryden complained that he could not write a character-poem on commission.
literary_significance: An important experiment in the 'character' as a poetic form and a revealing document of Dryden's professional circumstances in the 1690s.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1692. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958).

title: Fables Ancient and Modern
description: Dryden's last volume, a collection of verse translations and adaptations from Homer, Ovid, Boccaccio, and Chaucer, dedicated to the Duke of Ormond and prefaced by his famous account of translation.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains, among others, Palamon and Arcite (from Boccaccio's Teseida), The Cock and the Fox (from Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale), The Wife of Bath Her Tale, Theodore and Honoria, Cymon and Iphigenia, and the twelfth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of narrative poems unified by the preface's theory of translation as the art of conveying a dead author's spirit in the living language.
principal_characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emily; Chaunticlere; Pertelote; Reynard; Theodore; Honoria; Cymon; Iphigenia; the Wife of Bath
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets throughout, including the celebrated octosyllabic-free Chaucerian adaptations rendered in five-beat lines.
historical_context: Published in March 1700, two months before Dryden's death, by subscription after he had been stripped of the laureateship in 1689.
literary_significance: The greatest achievement of Dryden's late career and a founding document of English translation theory; Palamon and Arcite and the preface are canonical texts in the history of Chaucer reception.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1700. Standard text: The Poems of John Dryden (James Kinsley, ed., OUP, 1958); The Works of John Dryden, vols. VII-XI (California, 1966- ).

title: The Works of Virgil Translated into English Verse
alternative_titles: The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Aeneis
description: Dryden's complete translation of Virgil — the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the Aeneid — undertaken over more than a decade and published by subscription in three folio volumes in 1697.
plot_or_argument: A translation of all of Virgil: ten pastoral eclogues, four books of didactic georgic poetry, and the twelve-book epic of Aeneas's journey from Troy to the foundation of the Roman race.
narrative_structure: Three sections following Virgil's own tripartite oeuvre; Dryden's prefatory essays on pastoral, georgic, and epic theory accompany each.
principal_characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Tityrus; Meliboeus; Aristaeus
literary_form: epic translation; pastoral translation; didactic translation
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets throughout; Dryden's translation method is 'paraphrase' — sense for sense rather than word for word.
historical_context: Begun after Dryden lost his laureateship in 1689 and completed as his chief source of income; the subscription edition raised some £1,300, an unprecedented sum for a translation.
literary_significance: The dominant English Virgil for over two centuries and a decisive influence on the Augustan verse style; Johnson judged it 'such a translation as no age or nation could hope to see again'.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1697, Tonson, 3 vols. folio. Standard text: The Works of Virgil Translated by John Dryden (California edition of the Works of John Dryden, vols. III-VI, 1987).

title: The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis and Aulus Persius Flaccus
alternative_titles: The Satires of Juvenal and Persius
description: Dryden's translation of Juvenal's sixteen satires and Persius's six, prefaced by his long Discourse Concerning the Original and Progress of Satire, the foundational English treatise on the genre.
plot_or_argument: The Discourse distinguishes the 'Varronian' Menippean satire from formal verse satire, classifies formal satire into the delicate Horatian, the severe Persian, and the copious Juvenalian modes, and defends the last as suited to a corrupt age.
narrative_structure: A critical preface followed by the translated satires, Juvenal's Satire I and Persius's Satire VI being Dryden's own work and the rest by his sons and collaborators.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets.
historical_context: Published in 1693, in the Catholic exile of James II's court and at the height of the controversy over the ancients and moderns.
literary_significance: Its preface supplied the vocabulary of eighteenth-century satire criticism and directly shaped Pope's self-understanding; it remains the standard early modern English account of the genre.
attribution_notes: Dryden translated Juvenal I, VII-XVI and Persius VI; the remainder by Charles, John, and Henry Dryden and others; the Discourse is entirely Dryden's.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1693, Tonson. Standard text: The Works of John Dryden, vols. IV-V (California, 1974- ).

title: Hudibras
description: Samuel Butler's mock-heroic satire in three parts on Presbyterian and Independent hypocrisy, following the knight-errant Hudibras and his squire Ralpho through a series of absurd adventures in the wake of the Restoration.
plot_or_argument: Hudibras, a Puritan knight of absurd learning and courage, sets out with his squire Ralpho to suppress bear-baiting, is beaten by the widow's champion Trulla, is rescued by the astrologer Sidrophel, and courts the wealthy widow; each part satirises a different aspect of sectary enthusiasm.
narrative_structure: Three parts in eight cantos each, a picaresque sequence of digressive episodes with extensive marginal notes and a prose epistle.
principal_characters: Sir Hudibras; Ralpho; Trulla; Magnano; Cerdon; Sidrophel; Whachum; the Widow; Talgol; Orsin
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets with grotesque double and triple rhymes, deliberately anti-heroic; the 'Hudibrastic' verse.
historical_context: Part I published 1663, Part II 1664, Part III 1678; written from Butler's experience as secretary to the Presbyterian Sir Samuel Luke during the civil wars.
literary_significance: The most popular poem of the Restoration — Charles II carried a copy in his pocket — and the principal English model of low mock-heroic, influencing Swift, Pope's Dunciad, and the whole tradition of comic verse satire.
attribution_notes: Part I published anonymously but immediately ascribed to Butler; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: Parts I-III published 1663, 1664, 1678; Butler's Genuine Remains printed posthumously 1759. Standard edition: Hudibras (John Wilders, ed., Oxford University Press, 1967).

title: Miscellaneous Thoughts and Posthumous Works of Samuel Butler
alternative_titles: The Genuine Remains in Verse and Prose of Mr. Samuel Butler
description: Butler's posthumous collection of notebook verses, characters, letters, and prose satires, including 'The Elephant in the Moon', printed from his manuscripts long after his death in 1680.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers Butler's satirical characters (a set of prose portraits in the tradition of Theophrastus), his philosophical squibs against the Royal Society, and longer poems such as the lunar fable.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of prose characters, notes, letters, and verse satires.
meter_and_prosody: Mixed: prose characters and octosyllabic verse satires.
historical_context: Butler's notebooks passed to William Longueville and were printed as The Genuine Remains in 1759 by John Thyer; some pieces are of doubtful authenticity.
literary_significance: 'The Elephant in the Moon' is a notable early satire on the new experimental philosophy, and the characters are an important link between Earle's Microcosmographie and Addison's Spectator papers.
attribution_notes: Printed from manuscripts attributed to Butler; a small number of pieces are of doubtful authenticity.
bibliographical_notes: The Genuine Remains in Verse and Prose of Mr. Samuel Butler (London, 1759), 2 vols. Standard edition: The Miscellaneous Works of Samuel Butler (Henry Festing Jones, ed., Macmillan, 1887).

title: A Satire Against Reason and Mankind
alternative_titles: A Satyr Against Reason and Mankind
description: Rochester's most substantial philosophical poem, a libertine dialogue between a satirist who would rather be a dog than a man and a clergyman who defends reason, in which 'right reason' is reduced to the guidance of appetite.
plot_or_argument: The poet attacks the pride and falsity of human reason; the bishop replies in defence of reason as the light of God; the poet answers by distinguishing true reason, which serves the senses, from speculative reason, which is mere fear and fancy.
narrative_structure: A dramatic dialogue in two unequal parts, closing with the poet's self-portrait of the man of sense and pleasure.
principal_characters: the speaker; the bishop (Thomas Sprat, according to tradition)
meter_and_prosody: Irregular pentameter couplets, colloquial and argumentative.
historical_context: Composed c. 1674-5 and circulated in manuscript in the court coterie; Rochester's Hobbesian scepticism answers the Cambridge Platonists and the new natural philosophy.
literary_significance: The most intellectually serious poem of Restoration libertinism and a central text for understanding Rochester's rehabilitation in the late twentieth century.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Rochester in contemporary manuscript witnesses; authorship accepted, though individual lines vary between witnesses.
bibliographical_notes: Circulated in manuscript; first printed in Poems on Several Occasions (1716). Standard edition: The Poems and Life of John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester (David M. Vieth, ed., University of Chicago Press, 1968).

title: Poems on Several Occasions (Rochester)
description: The collected verse of John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester, issued in the year of his death, containing the satires, songs, and obscene verses that made him the most notorious poet of the Restoration court.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers Rochester's satires on the court and on Charles II ('I dreamt last night, though not designed to do so'), his songs including 'The Disabled Debauchee' and 'To a Lady in a Letter', his versified letters, and the bawdy lampoons.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of satires, songs, epistles, and lampoons; the 1680 edition includes the prose speech on the death of Colonel Blood.
meter_and_prosody: Varied: heroic couplets in the satires, song stanzas and octosyllables in the lyrics.
historical_context: Rochester's verse circulated mainly in manuscript within the court coterie; the 1680 edition was pirated and unauthorised, and the canon has been established only by modern editorial work on the manuscripts.
literary_significance: Rochester is now recognised as the most original English poet between Milton and Pope; his combination of Horatian ease with Hobbesian materialism anticipates the eighteenth century and the modern lyric of disillusion.
attribution_notes: The 1680 and 1716 printed collections contain pieces of doubtful authenticity; Vieth's 1968 edition establishes the canon from manuscript witnesses.
bibliographical_notes: Poems on Several Occasions (Antwerp [London], 1680). Standard edition: The Poems and Life of John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester (David M. Vieth, ed., University of Chicago Press, 1968); The Works of John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester (Harold Love, ed., Blackwell, 1999).

title: Songs and Poems of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
alternative_titles: The Works of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
description: The small but influential body of verse by the Earl of Dorset — courtier, wit, and patron — including the famous sea-song 'To all you ladies now at land', written, according to tradition, the night before the battle of Solebay.
plot_or_argument: The poems are light, graceful lyrics of love and parting, several written on public occasions and to particular women of the court; the sea-song consoles the ladies ashore while the men fight at sea.
narrative_structure: A short miscellany of songs and occasional verse.
meter_and_prosody: Short song stanzas in an easy, colloquial register.
historical_context: Dorset's verse circulated in manuscript at the court of Charles II; he was a leading patron of Dryden and Prior and a central figure in Restoration literary society.
literary_significance: 'To all you ladies now at land' became one of the best-known songs of the period; Dorset's work is a touchstone for the ideal of effortless courtly wit.
attribution_notes: The canon is small and some attributions are uncertain; the sea-song is traditionally ascribed to Dorset.
bibliographical_notes: First collected in The Works of the Earls of Rochester, Roscommon, and Dorset (London, 1714). Modern edition: The Poems of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset, in Poems on Affairs of State and in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography article.
